Dual Problem

Duality turns the transport problem into a search for potentials rather than couplings. This chapter explains why potentials certify optimality, how ccc-transforms regularize them, and why the quadratic case reveals convex analysis behind Brenier maps. Linear-programming duality gives the discrete picture Bertsimas & Tsitsiklis, 1997, while the continuous form is one of the central theorems of optimal transport Villani, 2003Santambrogio, 2015.

Discrete Dual¶

The discrete dual gives finite-dimensional certificates of optimality. Its complementary-slackness conditions identify where an optimal coupling can put mass.

Definition: Admissible Potentials

For a cost matrix C∈Rn×m\C\in\RR^{n\times m}C∈Rn×m and weights a∈Δna\in\simplex_na∈Δn​, b∈Δmb\in\simplex_mb∈Δm​, a pair (f,g)∈Rn×Rm(f,g)\in\RR^n\times\RR^m(f,g)∈Rn×Rm is admissible if it lies below the cost:

DC:={(f,g)∈Rn×Rm  :  fi+gj≤Cijfor all i,j}.\mathcal{D}_\C \eqdef \left\{ (f,g)\in\RR^n\times\RR^m \;:\; f_i+g_j\le \C_{ij} \quad\text{for all } i,j \right\}.DC​:={(f,g)∈Rn×Rm:fi​+gj​≤Cij​for all i,j}.
(1)

Equivalently, f⊕g≤Cf\oplus g\le \Cf⊕g≤C entrywise.

The two vectors play the role of source and target prices; admissibility means that no transported pair is priced above its travel cost. The discrete Kantorovich problem is a linear program. Hence its value can be computed either by minimizing over couplings or by maximizing over a pair of dual vectors.

Proposition: Discrete Kantorovich Duality

For a cost matrix C∈Rn×m\C\in\RR^{n\times m}C∈Rn×m and weights a∈Δna\in\simplex_na∈Δn​, b∈Δmb\in\simplex_mb∈Δm​,

LC(a,b)=max⁡(f,g)∈DC⟨f,a⟩+⟨g,b⟩.\mathcal{L}_\C(a,b) = \max_{(f,g)\in\mathcal{D}_\C} \langle f,a\rangle+\langle g,b\rangle.LC​(a,b)=(f,g)∈DC​max​⟨f,a⟩+⟨g,b⟩.
(2)
Proof

Start from the primal problem

min⁡P≥0,  P1m=a,  P⊤1n=b⟨C,P⟩\min_{\P\ge0,\;\P\mathbf{1}_m=a,\;\P^\top\mathbf{1}_n=b} \langle \C,\P\rangleP≥0,P1m​=a,P⊤1n​=bmin​⟨C,P⟩
(3)

Introduce multipliers (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) for its two marginal constraints. The Lagrangian is

L(P,f,g)=⟨C,P⟩+⟨a−P1m,f⟩+⟨b−P⊤1n,g⟩.\mathcal L(\P,f,g) = \langle \C,\P\rangle +\langle a-\P\mathbf{1}_m,f\rangle +\langle b-\P^\top\mathbf{1}_n,g\rangle .L(P,f,g)=⟨C,P⟩+⟨a−P1m​,f⟩+⟨b−P⊤1n​,g⟩.
(4)

For fixed potentials, the dual function is

inf⁡P≥0L(P,f,g)=⟨a,f⟩+⟨b,g⟩+inf⁡P≥0⟨C−(f⊕g),P⟩.\inf_{\P\ge0}\mathcal L(\P,f,g) = \langle a,f\rangle+\langle b,g\rangle +\inf_{\P\ge0}\langle \C-(f\oplus g),\P\rangle.P≥0inf​L(P,f,g)=⟨a,f⟩+⟨b,g⟩+P≥0inf​⟨C−(f⊕g),P⟩.
(5)

The last infimum is zero when Cij−fi−gj≥0\C_{ij}-f_i-g_j\ge0Cij​−fi​−gj​≥0 for all i,ji,ji,j, and −∞-\infty−∞ otherwise. The primal coupling polytope is nonempty because it contains a⊗ba\otimes ba⊗b, and it is compact. Finite-dimensional linear-programming strong duality and attainment therefore give (2).

Proposition: Discrete Complementary Slackness

For every feasible plan P\PP and admissible pair (f,g)(f,g)(f,g),

⟨C,P⟩−⟨f,a⟩−⟨g,b⟩=∑i,jPij(Cij−fi−gj)≥0.\langle \C,\P\rangle-\langle f,a\rangle-\langle g,b\rangle = \sum_{i,j}\P_{ij}(\C_{ij}-f_i-g_j)\ge0.⟨C,P⟩−⟨f,a⟩−⟨g,b⟩=i,j∑​Pij​(Cij​−fi​−gj​)≥0.
(6)

They are primal and dual optimal if and only if

supp⁡(P)⊂{(i,j):fi+gj=Cij}.\operatorname{supp}(\P) \subset \left\{(i,j): f_i+g_j=\C_{ij}\right\}.supp(P)⊂{(i,j):fi​+gj​=Cij​}.
(7)
Proof

The marginal constraints give ⟨f,a⟩+⟨g,b⟩=∑i,jPij(fi+gj)\langle f,a\rangle+\langle g,b\rangle =\sum_{i,j}\P_{ij}(f_i+g_j)⟨f,a⟩+⟨g,b⟩=∑i,j​Pij​(fi​+gj​), proving the gap identity. All summands are nonnegative. If the two feasible objects are optimal, strong duality makes their gap zero, so every summand with Pij>0\P_{ij}>0Pij​>0 vanishes. Conversely, the contact condition makes the gap zero and weak duality forces optimality.

Thus potentials are not transport maps themselves. They are certificates, and their equality set with the cost matrix is where an optimal coupling is allowed to place mass.

The formula (2) also shows that (a,b)↦LC(a,b)(a,b)\mapsto\mathcal{L}_\C(a,b)(a,b)↦LC​(a,b) is convex, being a supremum of linear functions. From the primal formulation, C↦LC(a,b)\C\mapsto\mathcal{L}_\C(a,b)C↦LC​(a,b) is concave.

General Formulation¶

The continuous dual is the analytic counterpart of the discrete linear program. It uses continuous potentials because measures are naturally probed through integration.

Continuous Duality¶

The finite-dimensional price vectors become continuous test functions. The pairing is ⟨f,α⟩:=∫f  dα\langle f,\alpha\rangle\eqdef\int f\,\d\alpha⟨f,α⟩:=∫fdα.

Proposition: Kantorovich Duality

Assume that X\XX and Y\YY are compact metric spaces and that c∈C(X×Y)c\in\Cc(\X\times\Y)c∈C(X×Y). Then

Lc(α,β)=max⁡(f,g)∈Dc∫Xf(x)  dα(x)+∫Yg(y)  dβ(y),\mathcal{L}_c(\alpha,\beta) = \max_{(f,g)\in\mathcal{D}_c} \int_\X f(x)\,\d\alpha(x) + \int_\Y g(y)\,\d\beta(y),Lc​(α,β)=(f,g)∈Dc​max​∫X​f(x)dα(x)+∫Y​g(y)dβ(y),
(8)

where

Dc:={(f,g)∈C(X)×C(Y)  :  f(x)+g(y)≤c(x,y)for all (x,y)}.\mathcal{D}_c \eqdef \left\{ (f,g)\in\Cc(\X)\times\Cc(\Y) \;:\; f(x)+g(y)\le c(x,y) \quad\text{for all }(x,y) \right\}.Dc​:={(f,g)∈C(X)×C(Y):f(x)+g(y)≤c(x,y)for all (x,y)}.
(9)

The same formula extends under the usual lower-semicontinuity and integrability assumptions, replacing maxima by suprema when dual optimizers need not exist.

Proof

Weak duality is immediate. If f(x)+g(y)≤c(x,y)f(x)+g(y)\le c(x,y)f(x)+g(y)≤c(x,y) and π∈Π(α,β)\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)π∈Π(α,β), then

∫f  dα+∫g  dβ=∫(f(x)+g(y))  dπ(x,y)≤∫c(x,y)  dπ(x,y).\int f\,\d\alpha+\int g\,\d\beta = \int (f(x)+g(y))\,\d\pi(x,y) \le \int c(x,y)\,\d\pi(x,y).∫fdα+∫gdβ=∫(f(x)+g(y))dπ(x,y)≤∫c(x,y)dπ(x,y).
(10)

Taking the supremum over admissible potentials and the infimum over couplings gives the first inequality.

For the reverse inequality, let V=Lc(α,β)V=\mathcal L_c(\alpha,\beta)V=Lc​(α,β) and consider the cone

K={(π1,π2,∫c  dπ+r):π∈M+(X×Y), r≥0}.\mathcal K= \left\{ \left(\pi_1,\pi_2,\int c\,\d\pi+r\right) : \pi\in\mathcal M_+(\X\times\Y),\ r\ge0 \right\}.K={(π1​,π2​,∫cdπ+r):π∈M+​(X×Y), r≥0}.
(11)

The cone is closed in the product weak topology: convergence of one marginal bounds the masses, compactness provides a weakly convergent subnet, and continuity of marginalization and of π↦∫c  dπ\pi\mapsto\int c\,\d\piπ↦∫cdπ identifies its limit. For t<Vt<Vt<V, the point zt=(α,β,t)z_t=(\alpha,\beta,t)zt​=(α,β,t) is not in K\mathcal KK. Strong separation gives F∈C(X)F\in\Cc(\X)F∈C(X), G∈C(Y)G\in\Cc(\Y)G∈C(Y) and λ∈R\lambda\in\RRλ∈R such that

∫F  dα+∫G  dβ+λt<0≤∫F  dη+∫G  dζ+λsfor all (η,ζ,s)∈K.\int F\,\d\alpha+\int G\,\d\beta+\lambda t<0 \le \int F\,\d\eta+\int G\,\d\zeta+\lambda s \quad \text{for all }(\eta,\zeta,s)\in\mathcal K.∫Fdα+∫Gdβ+λt<0≤∫Fdη+∫Gdζ+λsfor all (η,ζ,s)∈K.
(12)

Testing (0,0,r)(0,0,r)(0,0,r) gives λ≥0\lambda\ge0λ≥0, and testing Dirac generators gives F(x)+G(y)+λc(x,y)≥0F(x)+G(y)+\lambda c(x,y)\ge0F(x)+G(y)+λc(x,y)≥0. If λ=0\lambda=0λ=0, integration against α⊗β\alpha\otimes\betaα⊗β contradicts strict separation, so λ>0\lambda>0λ>0. Therefore f=−F/λf=-F/\lambdaf=−F/λ and g=−G/λg=-G/\lambdag=−G/λ are admissible and have dual value greater than ttt. Letting t↑Vt\uparrow Vt↑V proves equality.

For attainment, take a maximizing sequence and successively set

g~k(y)=min⁡x{c(x,y)−fk(x)},f~k(x)=min⁡y{c(x,y)−g~k(y)}.\widetilde g_k(y)=\min_x\{c(x,y)-f_k(x)\}, \qquad \widetilde f_k(x)=\min_y\{c(x,y)-\widetilde g_k(y)\}.g​k​(y)=xmin​{c(x,y)−fk​(x)},f​k​(x)=ymin​{c(x,y)−g​k​(y)}.
(13)

These replacements preserve feasibility and improve the objective. Normalize f~k(x0)=0\widetilde f_k(x_0)=0f​k​(x0​)=0. The envelopes inherit the uniform moduli of ccc in the two variables and are uniformly bounded. Arzela--Ascoli gives a uniformly convergent maximizing subsequence, whose limit remains admissible.

Remark: Dual attainment from ccc-transforms

The final part of the proof uses the ccc-transforms introduced below. A continuous cost on a compact product has uniform moduli in both variables, and transformed potentials inherit them by Proposition Proposition: Modulus Stability Of ccc-Transforms. Lipschitz costs give equi-Lipschitz potentials as a special case, but Lipschitz continuity is not required for attainment.

Complementary Slackness¶

As in the finite problem, equality of primal and dual values localizes the support of every optimal coupling.

Proposition: Continuous Complementary Slackness

For π∈Π(α,β)\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)π∈Π(α,β) and admissible (f,g)(f,g)(f,g),

∫c  dπ−∫f  dα−∫g  dβ=∫(c(x,y)−f(x)−g(y))  dπ(x,y)≥0.\int c\,\d\pi-\int f\,\d\alpha-\int g\,\d\beta = \int\bigl(c(x,y)-f(x)-g(y)\bigr)\,\d\pi(x,y)\ge0.∫cdπ−∫fdα−∫gdβ=∫(c(x,y)−f(x)−g(y))dπ(x,y)≥0.
(14)

The coupling and potentials are optimal if and only if the gap vanishes. In that case,

supp⁡(π)⊂{(x,y):f(x)+g(y)=c(x,y)}.\operatorname{supp}(\pi) \subset \left\{(x,y):f(x)+g(y)=c(x,y)\right\}.supp(π)⊂{(x,y):f(x)+g(y)=c(x,y)}.
(15)
Proof

The marginal identities give the equality, and admissibility gives nonnegativity. A zero gap is equivalent to equality of feasible primal and dual values. The slack is continuous and nonnegative; if it were positive at a point of supp⁡(π)\operatorname{supp}(\pi)supp(π), it would have positive integral on a neighborhood of that point.

The discrete case corresponds to dual vectors that sample the continuous potentials, (fi,gj)=(f(xi),g(yj))(f_i,g_j)=(f(x_i),g(y_j))(fi​,gj​)=(f(xi​),g(yj​)).

For the one-dimensional quadratic cost, the continuous potentials can be read from the monotone map T=Fβ−1∘FαT=F_\beta^{-1}\circ F_\alphaT=Fβ−1​∘Fα​: on the active graph, f′(x)=2(x−T(x))f'(x)=2(x-T(x))f′(x)=2(x−T(x)) and g=fcg=f^cg=fc.

In contrast to the primal problem, dual attainment is not immediate: the constraint set is not compact and the objective is not coercive. The ccc-transform selects canonical representatives that inherit the modulus of continuity of the cost; a gauge condition then makes the family compact.

c-Transforms¶

The ccc-transform is the operation that improves potentials without changing feasibility. It is both a proof device for dual attainment and the route from duality to Brenier’s convex potentials.

Best-Response Potentials¶

Keeping a dual potential fff fixed, one can maximize in closed form over the second potential in the dual problem:

sup⁡g{∫g  dβ  :  g(y)≤c(x,y)−f(x)for all x,y}.\sup_g \left\{ \int g\,\d\beta \;:\; g(y)\le c(x,y)-f(x) \quad\text{for all }x,y \right\}.gsup​{∫gdβ:g(y)≤c(x,y)−f(x)for all x,y}.
(17)

The constraint is equivalent to g(y)≤fc(y)g(y)\le f^c(y)g(y)≤fc(y).

Definition: ccc-Transform

For a real-valued function f:X→Rf:\X\to\RRf:X→R, its ccc-transform is the extended-real-valued function

fc(y):=inf⁡x∈X{c(x,y)−f(x)}.f^c(y) \eqdef \inf_{x\in\X}\{c(x,y)-f(x)\}.fc(y):=x∈Xinf​{c(x,y)−f(x)}.
(18)

For a real-valued function g:Y→Rg:\Y\to\RRg:Y→R, the cˉ\bar ccˉ-transform associated with cˉ(y,x)=c(x,y)\bar c(y,x)=c(x,y)cˉ(y,x)=c(x,y) is

gcˉ(x):=inf⁡y∈Y{c(x,y)−g(y)}.g^{\bar c}(x) \eqdef \inf_{y\in\Y}\{c(x,y)-g(y)\}.gcˉ(x):=y∈Yinf​{c(x,y)−g(y)}.
(19)

On compact spaces, if ccc and the input potential are continuous, these infima are finite minima and the transformed potential is continuous.

Remark: Discrete ccc-transform

If α=∑i=1naiδxi\al=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\de_{x_i}α=∑i=1n​ai​δxi​​ and β=∑j=1mbjδyj\be=\sum_{j=1}^m b_j\de_{y_j}β=∑j=1m​bj​δyj​​, the same definition applies to the finite spaces X={xi}i\X=\{x_i\}_iX={xi​}i​ and Y={yj}j\Y=\{y_j\}_jY={yj​}j​. The dual potentials are then vectors (f,g)∈Rn×Rm(\fD,\gD)\in\RR^n\times\RR^m(f,g)∈Rn×Rm, as in Section Discrete Dual, and the cost is the matrix C∈Rn×m\C\in\RR^{n\times m}C∈Rn×m with entries

Ci,j=c(xi,yj).\C_{i,j}=c(x_i,y_j).Ci,j​=c(xi​,yj​).
(20)

With the present sign convention f⊕g≤cf\oplus g\leq cf⊕g≤c, the discrete transform of f\fDf is the vector fC∈Rm\fD^\C\in\RR^mfC∈Rm defined by

(fC)j=min⁡1≤i≤nCi,j−fi.(\fD^\C)_j = \min_{1\leq i\leq n} \C_{i,j}-\fD_i.(fC)j​=1≤i≤nmin​Ci,j​−fi​.
(21)

This is a minimum because feasibility imposes the upper bound gj≤Ci,j−fi\gD_j\leq \C_{i,j}-\fD_igj​≤Ci,j​−fi​ for every iii. Thus the largest feasible best response is the minimum of these upper bounds; formulas with a maximum correspond to a different sign convention, not to the dual constraint (2). With Cˉ:=C⊤\bar\C\eqdef\C^\topCˉ:=C⊤, the opposite transform of g\gDg is

gCˉ:=gC⊤∈Rn,(gCˉ)i=min⁡1≤j≤mCi,j−gj.\gD^{\bar\C}\eqdef \gD^{\C^\top}\in\RR^n, \qquad (\gD^{\bar\C})_i = \min_{1\leq j\leq m} \C_{i,j}-\gD_j.gCˉ:=gC⊤∈Rn,(gCˉ)i​=1≤j≤mmin​Ci,j​−gj​.
(22)

Thus the continuous best-response operation reduces exactly to taking column minima for fC\fD^\CfC, or row minima for gCˉ\gD^{\bar\C}gCˉ, in shifted cost matrices. Chapter Paragraph studies the hybrid case where α\alα has a density and β\beβ is discrete; then gcˉ(x)=min⁡jc(x,yj)−gjg^{\bar c}(x)=\min_j c(x,y_j)-g_jgcˉ(x)=minj​c(x,yj​)−gj​ is a lower envelope over target atoms, and the regions where each atom realizes the minimum are the Laguerre cells for the quadratic cost.

Since β\betaβ is nonnegative, maximizing ∫g  dβ\int g\,\d\beta∫gdβ is achieved by taking g=fcg=f^cg=fc on the support of β\betaβ, equivalently β\betaβ-almost everywhere.

Proposition: ccc-Transforms Solve The Semi-Relaxed Problems

Under the compactness and continuity hypotheses above, for fixed f∈C(X)f\in\Cc(\X)f∈C(X) the maximizers of the dual objective over all g∈C(Y)g\in\Cc(\Y)g∈C(Y) such that f⊕g≤cf\oplus g\le cf⊕g≤c are exactly the functions satisfying g=fcg=f^cg=fc β\betaβ-almost everywhere. Equivalently,

inf⁡π∈M+1(X×Y)π2=β∫c(x,y)  dπ(x,y)−∫f(x)  dπ1(x)=∫fc(y)  dβ(y).\inf_{\substack{\pi\in\mathcal M_+^1(\X\times\Y)\\\pi_2=\beta}} \int c(x,y)\,\d\pi(x,y)-\int f(x)\,\d\pi_1(x) = \int f^c(y)\,\d\beta(y).π∈M+1​(X×Y)π2​=β​inf​∫c(x,y)dπ(x,y)−∫f(x)dπ1​(x)=∫fc(y)dβ(y).
(23)

Symmetrically, for fixed ggg, the maximizers over fff satisfy f=gcˉf=g^{\bar c}f=gcˉ α\alphaα-almost everywhere.

Proof

The constraint f(x)+g(y)≤c(x,y)f(x)+g(y)\le c(x,y)f(x)+g(y)≤c(x,y) for all xxx is equivalent, for each fixed yyy, to

g(y)≤inf⁡xc(x,y)−f(x)=fc(y).g(y)\le \inf_x c(x,y)-f(x)=f^c(y).g(y)≤xinf​c(x,y)−f(x)=fc(y).
(24)

Since β\betaβ is nonnegative, the largest possible value of ∫g  dβ\int g\,\d\beta∫gdβ is obtained by saturating this pointwise upper bound on the support of β\betaβ. The proof for f=gcˉf=g^{\bar c}f=gcˉ is identical after exchanging the two marginals.

For the primal formula, disintegrate any feasible plan as π( dx, dy)=πy( dx)β( dy)\pi(\d x,\d y)=\pi_y(\d x)\beta(\d y)π(dx,dy)=πy​(dx)β(dy). Then

∫c  dπ−∫f  dπ1=∫(∫(c(x,y)−f(x))  dπy(x)) dβ(y)≥∫fc(y)  dβ(y).\int c\,\d\pi-\int f\,\d\pi_1 = \int \left( \int (c(x,y)-f(x))\,\d\pi_y(x) \right)\d\beta(y) \ge \int f^c(y)\,\d\beta(y).∫cdπ−∫fdπ1​=∫(∫(c(x,y)−f(x))dπy​(x))dβ(y)≥∫fc(y)dβ(y).
(25)

The argmin sets are nonempty and compact, and the measurable maximum theorem provides a Borel selector x⋆(y)x_\star(y)x⋆​(y). The coupling π( dx, dy)=δx⋆(y)( dx)β( dy)\pi(\d x,\d y)=\delta_{x_\star(y)}(\d x)\beta(\d y)π(dx,dy)=δx⋆​(y)​(dx)β(dy) attains equality.

The updates must be sequential:

(f,g)⟼(f,fc)⟼(fccˉ,fc).(f,g)\longmapsto(f,f^c) \longmapsto(f^{c\bar c},f^c).(f,g)⟼(f,fc)⟼(fccˉ,fc).
(26)

Each step preserves feasibility and improves the objective. Simultaneously replacing an arbitrary old pair by (gcˉ,fc)(g^{\bar c},f^c)(gcˉ,fc) need not preserve feasibility, because the two best responses were computed against different old coordinates. For example, if c≡0c\equiv0c≡0 and f=g≡−1f=g\equiv-1f=g≡−1, both transforms equal 1 and their simultaneous update violates the dual constraint. Functions of the form fcf^cfc and gcˉg^{\bar c}gcˉ are called ccc-concave and cˉ\bar ccˉ-concave, respectively.

Proposition: Modulus Stability Of ccc-Transforms

If

∣c(x,y)−c(x,y′)∣≤ωY(dY(y,y′))|c(x,y)-c(x,y')| \le\omega_\Y(d_\Y(y,y'))∣c(x,y)−c(x,y′)∣≤ωY​(dY​(y,y′))
(27)

uniformly in xxx, then every finite fcf^cfc has modulus ωY\omega_\YωY​. The symmetric statement holds for gcˉg^{\bar c}gcˉ in the first variable. In particular, a uniform LLL-Lipschitz bound on the cost gives an LLL-Lipschitz transform.

Proof

For each xxx, set Fx(y)=c(x,y)−f(x)F_x(y)=c(x,y)-f(x)Fx​(y)=c(x,y)−f(x) and F(y)=fc(y)=inf⁡xFx(y)F(y)=f^c(y)=\inf_x F_x(y)F(y)=fc(y)=infx​Fx​(y). Since all functions FxF_xFx​ share the same modulus,

∣F(y)−F(y′)∣=∣inf⁡xFx(y)−inf⁡xFx(y′)∣≤sup⁡x∣Fx(y)−Fx(y′)∣≤ωY(dY(y,y′)).|F(y)-F(y')| = \left|\inf_x F_x(y)-\inf_x F_x(y')\right| \le \sup_x |F_x(y)-F_x(y')| \le \omega_\Y(d_\Y(y,y')).∣F(y)−F(y′)∣=∣∣​xinf​Fx​(y)−xinf​Fx​(y′)∣∣​≤xsup​∣Fx​(y)−Fx​(y′)∣≤ωY​(dY​(y,y′)).
(28)

The proof in the first variable is identical.

This stability is crucial for dual attainment. On compact spaces, continuity of ccc already supplies uniform moduli; sequential closure and a harmless additive gauge then give compactness by Arzela--Ascoli.

Euclidean Case¶

The Euclidean quadratic cost is the model case where ccc-transforms become ordinary convex conjugates after removing quadratic terms. This is the algebraic bridge between Kantorovich duality and Brenier maps.

Normalize the quadratic cost as q(x,y)=12∥x−y∥2q(x,y)=\frac12\norm{x-y}^2q(x,y)=21​∥x−y∥2. For any π∈Π(α,β)\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)π∈Π(α,β),

∫q(x,y)  dπ(x,y)=12∫∥x∥2  dα(x)+12∫∥y∥2  dβ(y)−∫⟨x,y⟩  dπ(x,y).\int q(x,y)\,\d\pi(x,y) = \frac12\int\norm{x}^2\,\d\alpha(x) + \frac12\int\norm{y}^2\,\d\beta(y) -\int \langle x,y\rangle\,\d\pi(x,y).∫q(x,y)dπ(x,y)=21​∫∥x∥2dα(x)+21​∫∥y∥2dβ(y)−∫⟨x,y⟩dπ(x,y).
(29)

The first two terms depend only on the marginals, so quadratic OT reduces to c(x,y)=−⟨x,y⟩c(x,y)=-\langle x,y\ranglec(x,y)=−⟨x,y⟩. For this bilinear cost,

fc(y)=inf⁡x−⟨x,y⟩−f(x)=−(−f)∗(y),h∗(y):=sup⁡x⟨x,y⟩−h(x).f^c(y) = \inf_x -\langle x,y\rangle-f(x) = -(-f)^*(y), \qquad h^*(y)\eqdef\sup_x \langle x,y\rangle-h(x).fc(y)=xinf​−⟨x,y⟩−f(x)=−(−f)∗(y),h∗(y):=xsup​⟨x,y⟩−h(x).
(30)

On full Euclidean space, fccˉ=−(−f)∗∗f^{c\bar c}=-(-f)^{**}fccˉ=−(−f)∗∗. Hence ccc-closed functions are negatives of lower semicontinuous convex functions, and closure gives the smallest upper semicontinuous concave majorant. On restricted compact domains, the supporting slopes must additionally belong to the opposite domain.

Remark: Proof of Brenier’s theorem

Let α,β∈P2(Rd)\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal P_2(\RR^d)α,β∈P2​(Rd) and assume that α\alphaα has a density. For q(x,y)=12∥x−y∥2q(x,y)=\frac12\norm{x-y}^2q(x,y)=21​∥x−y∥2, let (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) be a closed optimal dual pair and set

ϕ(x)=12∥x∥2−u(x),ψ(y)=12∥y∥2−v(y).\phi(x)=\frac12\norm{x}^2-u(x), \qquad \psi(y)=\frac12\norm{y}^2-v(y).ϕ(x)=21​∥x∥2−u(x),ψ(y)=21​∥y∥2−v(y).
(31)

The dual constraint becomes ϕ(x)+ψ(y)≥⟨x,y⟩\phi(x)+\psi(y)\ge\langle x,y\rangleϕ(x)+ψ(y)≥⟨x,y⟩. The two closure relations give ψ=ϕ∗\psi=\phi^*ψ=ϕ∗ and ϕ=ψ∗\phi=\psi^*ϕ=ψ∗, so ϕ\phiϕ is convex. Complementary slackness shows that an optimal plan satisfies

supp⁡(π)⊂{(x,y):ϕ(x)+ϕ∗(y)=⟨x,y⟩}.\operatorname{supp}(\pi) \subset \left\{(x,y):\phi(x)+\phi^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle\right\}.supp(π)⊂{(x,y):ϕ(x)+ϕ∗(y)=⟨x,y⟩}.
(32)

Fenchel equality is equivalent to y∈∂ϕ(x)y\in\partial\phi(x)y∈∂ϕ(x). Convex functions are differentiable Lebesgue-almost everywhere, hence α\alphaα-almost everywhere, so the subdifferential is almost surely a singleton. This yields the Brenier map T=∇ϕT=\nabla\phiT=∇ϕ. Multiplying the cost by two rescales the potentials but does not change the map.

Why Hard Alternating Optimization Stops¶

A crucial property of the Legendre transform is that f∗∗∗=f∗f^{***}=f^*f∗∗∗=f∗, while f∗∗f^{**}f∗∗ is the lower semicontinuous convex envelope of a proper fff. Analogous identities explain why exact alternating best responses stop after one cycle for ccc-transforms Rockafellar, 2015.

Proposition: Algebra Of ccc-Transforms

The following identities hold, with inequalities understood pointwise:

(i) f≤f′⇒fc≥f′c,(ii) fccˉ≥f,\text{(i) } f\le f' \Rightarrow f^c\ge f'^c, \qquad \text{(ii) } f^{c\bar c}\ge f,(i) f≤f′⇒fc≥f′c,(ii) fccˉ≥f,
(33)
(iii) gcˉc≥g,(iv) fccˉc=fc.\text{(iii) } g^{\bar c c}\ge g, \qquad \text{(iv) } f^{c\bar c c}=f^c.(iii) gcˉc≥g,(iv) fccˉc=fc.
(34)
Proof

The first inequality follows directly from the minus sign. For every x,yx,yx,y,

fc(y)=inf⁡x′{c(x′,y)−f(x′)}≤c(x,y)−f(x).f^c(y)=\inf_{x'}\{c(x',y)-f(x')\} \le c(x,y)-f(x).fc(y)=x′inf​{c(x′,y)−f(x′)}≤c(x,y)−f(x).
(35)

Thus c(x,y)−fc(y)≥f(x)c(x,y)-f^c(y)\ge f(x)c(x,y)−fc(y)≥f(x), and taking the infimum over yyy proves (ii). The relation gcˉc≥gg^{\bar c c}\ge ggcˉc≥g is symmetric. To prove (iv), use order reversal with f≤fccˉf\le f^{c\bar c}f≤fccˉ to get fc≥fccˉcf^c\ge f^{c\bar c c}fc≥fccˉc. Applying (iii) to g=fcg=f^cg=fc gives the reverse inequality.

This invariance shows that exact block maximization reaches a coordinatewise fixed point after one full cycle:

(f,g)↦(f,fc)↦(fccˉ,fc)↦(fccˉ,fccˉc)=(fccˉ,fc).(f,g)\mapsto(f,f^c) \mapsto(f^{c\bar c},f^c) \mapsto(f^{c\bar c},f^{c\bar c c}) =(f^{c\bar c},f^c).(f,g)↦(f,fc)↦(fccˉ,fc)↦(fccˉ,fccˉc)=(fccˉ,fc).
(36)

The resulting pair is dual feasible but need not maximize the joint objective, because its value still depends on the arbitrary initial fff. Entropic regularization replaces hard minima by soft log-sum-exp responses and leads to the nontrivial Sinkhorn scaling iteration.

For c(x,y)=−xyc(x,y)=-xyc(x,y)=−xy on compact intervals, fccˉf^{c\bar c}fccˉ is the smallest concave majorant representable with slopes in the opposite interval. In the displayed example that interval contains every relevant supporting slope, so the restricted closure is the ordinary concave envelope.

In Figure Div, the displayed interval contains all relevant supporting slopes, so this restricted closure agrees with the ordinary concave envelope.

Hard ccc-transforms for the bilinear cost c(x,y)=−xyc(x,y)=-xyc(x,y)=−xy.
